mcqs.question: Why is a foreground Service granted more protection from being killed than a plain Service?
options: Foreground Services run in a separate, protected process managed by the OS kernel
Foreground Services cannot access the network, reducing their risk profile
Foreground Services are only allowed to run for a maximum of 30 seconds, which is inherently safer
The mandatory persistent notification gives the user visibility into and control over the work, which is the trust trade-off that earns the longer leash from the OS
mcqs.explanation: The notification requirement isn't cosmetic — it's the mechanism that justifies the elevated priority: the user can see the work is happening and force-stop it if needed, which is a fundamentally different trust model than invisible background work the user has no way to notice or intervene on.

mcqs.question: A WorkManager job is configured with setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.UNMETERED) and setRequiresCharging(true). What does this actually cause?
options: The job runs immediately regardless of network or charging state, using these as hints only
The job runs at the exact interval requested, checking these conditions only as a fallback

The job waits until the device is both on an unmetered connection (like WiFi) and charging before running, letting the OS batch it efficiently with other constrained work rather than running on a specific schedule
The job fails permanently if these conditions aren't met within 24 hours
mcqs.explanation: Constraints tell WorkManager to defer execution until all specified conditions are actually satisfied — the OS decides the exact moment, batching it with other apps' deferred work, which is the whole point of declaring constraints instead of forcing a specific execution time.

mcqs.question: A team uses a foreground Service purely to avoid WorkManager's deferred scheduling for a background sync job the user never actually sees running. Why is this a misuse of the mechanism?
options: Foreground Services are technically incapable of performing sync operations

This routes around the throttling deferrable work is meant to respect, using the escape hatch intended for genuine long-running, user-visible work to instead force immediate, unthrottled execution for something the user gets no actual visibility or benefit from
This will cause the app to be immediately banned from the app store
There's no real issue since foreground Services are always the safer choice
mcqs.explanation: Foreground Service protection is a trade-off — elevated priority in exchange for genuine user visibility via the mandatory notification — using it just to dodge WorkManager's throttling for work the user doesn't need to see is misusing that trade-off, forcing unthrottled execution while providing none of the transparency the mechanism assumes.

mcqs.question: An app enqueues a WorkManager job, and the device reboots before it runs. What happens to the job?
options: It is lost and must be manually re-enqueued by app code after the reboot
WorkManager jobs are only guaranteed to survive process death, not a full reboot
The job runs immediately at the moment of reboot, ignoring its original constraints

WorkManager persists enqueued work to an on-device database, so it survives the reboot and the OS reschedules and eventually runs it once its constraints are satisfiable again, with no extra code required
mcqs.explanation: WorkManager's core durability guarantee specifically covers both process death and device reboot — enqueued work is persisted, not held only in memory, so it's automatically rescheduled and run once constraints are met again, with no manual re-enqueueing needed.

mcqs.question: A team implements periodic background data sync using a plain Service left running, rather than WorkManager. What's the risk?
options: Plain Services run identically to WorkManager jobs, so there's no meaningful risk

The Service has no special exemption from background-execution limits and can be killed under memory pressure with little warning, and doesn't automatically survive process death or reboot the way WorkManager's persisted work does
Plain Services are deprecated and will fail to compile
The main risk is that plain Services cannot access the network at all
mcqs.explanation: A bare Service gets no special protection from the OS's general background-execution limits, and unlike WorkManager, it has no built-in persistence across process death or reboot — for genuinely deferrable, must-eventually-complete work, WorkManager was purpose-built to provide exactly the durability and constraint-based scheduling a plain Service lacks.

mcqs.question: A periodic WorkManager job with no constraints at all syncs data over the network every few hours. What's the risk of omitting constraints, even for lightweight work?
options: WorkManager will refuse to schedule an unconstrained periodic job
This has no practical effect since WorkManager always waits for WiFi automatically
Unconstrained jobs run twice as frequently as constrained ones

The job can run on a poor cellular connection, on a metered data plan, or when battery is nearly dead — exactly the conditions where network work is least welcome — since nothing tells the OS to wait for better conditions
mcqs.explanation: Without constraints, the OS runs the job whenever the periodic interval is due and the device is technically capable, with no guarantee of favorable network or power conditions — for anything touching the network, an explicit network-type or charging constraint is what actually protects the user from paying for it at the worst possible moment.
